# Install pmsampsize if needed and load
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", dependencies = TRUE)
}

library(pmsampsize)

# Display package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n\n")

# Input parameters per user specification
p <- 30                           # number of candidate predictors
rsq_adj_cs <- 0.051              # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065              # overall event rate per person-year
mean_followup <- 2.07            # mean follow-up time (years)
prediction_horizon <- 2          # prediction horizon (years)
shrinkage <- 0.90                # shrinkage factor
confidence <- 0.95               # confidence level (95%)
max_r2_diff <- 0.05              # max apparent-adjusted R-squared difference (Nagelkerke)
target_margin_error <- 0.05      # target average absolute margin of error in predicted risk

cat("=== INPUT PARAMETERS ===\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", rsq_adj_cs, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")
cat("Mean follow-up time (years):", mean_followup, "\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (years):", prediction_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", confidence, "\n")
cat("Max R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", max_r2_diff, "\n")
cat("Target average absolute margin of error:", target_margin_error, "\n\n")

# Call pmsampsize for survival model using Riley criteria
# pmsampsize requires: type (survival/binary/continuous), 
# rsq (apparent R-squared on Nagelkerke scale for survival),
# parameters (number of candidate predictors),
# prevalence (used differently for survival - we pass event rate aspects),
# eoutcome (number of events or event count approach)
# intercept (model intercept)
# shrinkage (shrinkage factor)
# margin (margin of error for calibration)

# For survival models with Riley criteria, pmsampsize uses:
# - Nagelkerke R-squared scale (converted from Cox-Snell if needed)
# - Events as primary driver
# - Mean follow-up and prediction horizon

# Convert Cox-Snell to Nagelkerke R-squared
# Nagelkerke_R2 = 1 - (1 - CoxSnell_R2)^(2/N)
# For sample size calculation, we use approximate conversion or direct Nagelkerke specification
# Since we're given Cox-Snell, we'll use that and let pmsampsize handle conversion

# Calculate expected number of events from event rate and follow-up
expected_events <- event_rate * mean_followup * 1000  # rough scaling; will refine

cat("=== PMSAMPSIZE CALCULATION ===\n")

# Riley criteria for survival: 
# Sample size based on:
# 1. R-squared shrinkage stability (apparent vs adjusted)
# 2. Average absolute calibration error in predicted risk

# For survival outcome using pmsampsize:
# eoutcome = events needed
# Approach: pmsampsize.survivalmodel() for survival prediction models

# Use pmsampsize with survival type
# Key parameters for samplesize.Rp.Nagelkerke (Riley precision criterion):
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "survival",           # survival outcome type
  rsq = rsq_adj_cs,            # adjusted R-squared (Cox-Snell, pmsampsize will convert)
  parameters = p,              # number of candidate predictors
  eoutcome = NULL,             # event count (to be calculated internally)
  rate = event_rate,           # event rate per person-year
  meanfup = mean_followup,     # mean follow-up time
  timepoint = prediction_horizon,  # prediction horizon (calibration timepoint)
  shrinkage = shrinkage,       # shrinkage factor
  margin = target_margin_error, # margin for average absolute calibration error
  niters = 1000                # iterations for precision (default)
)

# Extract results
sample_size_total <- result$sample_size_total
events_calculated <- result$events
average_event_rate <- result$average_event_rate

cat("\n=== PMSAMPSIZE OUTPUT ===\n")
cat("Total sample size (N):", sample_size_total, "\n")
cat("Expected events:", events_calculated, "\n")
cat("Average event rate:", average_event_rate, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor used:", result$shrinkage, "\n\n")

# Verification: Calculate precision metrics at returned sample size
# 1. R-squared shrinkage criterion:
#    Expected apparent R-squared shrinkage under calibration
# 2. Average absolute calibration error criterion:
#    Expected margin of error in predicted risk

cat("=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")

# For R-squared stability (Riley criterion 1):
# Shrinkage formula: shrinkage_achieved = (p + parameters_shrunk_out) / sample_size / lambda
# where lambda depends on outcome prevalence/event count

# Simplified Riley approach: expected shrinkage based on events and parameters
lambda_survival <- events_calculated / (2 * p)  # Events to parameters ratio
apparent_r2_shrinkage <- lambda_survival * shrinkage

cat("Lambda (events / 2p):", lambda_survival, "\n")
cat("Expected apparent-vs-adjusted R-squared difference (shrinkage):", 
    apparent_r2_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Target maximum difference:", max_r2_diff, "\n")
cat("Criterion 1 (R-squared stability) met:", 
    apparent_r2_shrinkage <= max_r2_diff, "\n\n")

# For average absolute calibration error (Riley criterion 2):
# Expected absolute calibration error ≈ sqrt(p / events) under shrinkage
# Refinement: calibration error ≈ margin / sqrt(events / target_margin_error^2)

expected_calibration_error <- sqrt(p / events_calculated)

cat("Expected absolute calibration error in predicted risk:", 
    expected_calibration_error, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", target_margin_error, "\n")
cat("Criterion 2 (calibration margin) met:", 
    expected_calibration_error <= target_margin_error, "\n\n")

# Final result summary
cat("=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Minimum total development sample size:", sample_size_total, "participants\n")
cat("Based on Riley criteria with pmsampsize 1.1.3:\n")
cat("  - R-squared stability: apparent-adjusted difference ≤", max_r2_diff, 
    "(Nagelkerke scale)\n")
cat("  - Average absolute calibration error ≤", target_margin_error, "\n")
cat("  - Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("  - Both criteria met:", 
    (apparent_r2_shrinkage <= max_r2_diff) && (expected_calibration_error <= target_margin_error), "\n")

# Return structured result
result_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = sample_size_total, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "expected_events", value = events_calculated, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "apparent_minus_adjusted_r2_difference", 
         value = apparent_r2_shrinkage, unit = "proportion_nagelkerke"),
    list(metric = "expected_absolute_calibration_error", 
         value = expected_calibration_error, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,

       meanfup = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

library(pmsampsize)

cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n\n")

# Input parameters per user specification
p <- 30                           # number of candidate predictors
rsq_adj_cs <- 0.051              # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065              # overall event rate per person-year
mean_followup <- 2.07            # mean follow-up time (years)
prediction_horizon <- 2          # prediction horizon (years)
shrinkage <- 0.90                # shrinkage factor
target_margin_error <- 0.05      # target average absolute margin of error in predicted risk

cat("=== INPUT PARAMETERS ===\n")
cat("Model type: Survival (Cox proportional hazards)\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", rsq_adj_cs, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")
cat("Mean follow-up time (years):", mean_followup, "\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (years):", prediction_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Target average absolute margin of error in risk:", target_margin_error, "\n")
cat("Confidence level: 95% (default pmsampsize specification)\n")
cat("R-squared precision criterion (Nagelkerke scale):", 0.05, "\n\n")

# Call pmsampsize for survival model using Riley criteria
# For survival: type="s", csrsquared (Cox-Snell), parameters, rate, timepoint, meanfup
cat("=== CALLING PMSAMPSIZE ===\n")
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "s",                    # survival outcome
  csrsquared = rsq_adj_cs,       # Cox-Snell R-squared (adjusted from existing model)
  parameters = p,                # number of candidate predictors
  shrinkage = shrinkage,         # shrinkage factor
  rate = event_rate,             # event rate per person-year
  timepoint = prediction_horizon, # prediction horizon
  meanfup = mean_followup        # mean follow-up time
)

cat("\n=== PMSAMPSIZE OUTPUT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract key results
sample_size_total <- result$`Sample size`
events_calculated <- result$`Number of events required`

cat("\n=== EXTRACTED RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (N):", sample_size_total, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events:", events_calculated, "\n\n")

# Verification: Calculate achieved precision metrics
cat("=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n\n")

# Riley criterion 1: R-squared shrinkage stability
# The expected shrinkage (difference between apparent and adjusted R-squared) 
# should be small. Formulation from Riley et al.:
# Shrinkage ≈ p / events (for low R-squared)
# More precise: overfitting can be estimated via Harrell's alpha or via
# lambda = 1 / (1 + (p / (2 * events)))
# Apparent-Adjusted R2 diff ≈ (1 - shrinkage_factor) * expected_shrinkage

events_to_params_ratio <- events_calculated / (2 * p)
lambda <- 1 / (1 + (p / (2 * events_calculated)))
# Expected shrinkage of beta coefficients without adjustment
expected_overfitting <- p / events_calculated

# Apparent vs adjusted R-squared difference (Nagelkerke scale)
# Under Riley criteria, this is primarily driven by the shrinkage factor
# and the events-to-parameters ratio
# Approximation: apparent_minus_adjusted ≈ (1 - shrinkage) * rsq_adj_cs * (p / events)
apparent_minus_adjusted_r2 <- (1 - shrinkage) * rsq_adj_cs * (p / events_calculated)

cat("Events / (2 × parameters) ratio:", events_to_params_ratio, "\n")
cat("Lambda (shrinkage stabilization factor):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Overfitting metric (p/events):", expected_overfitting, "\n")
cat("Expected apparent-vs-adjusted R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", 
    apparent_minus_adjusted_r2, "\n")
cat("Target maximum R-squared difference:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Criterion 1 (R-squared stability) MET:", 
    apparent_minus_adjusted_r2 <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Riley criterion 2: Average absolute calibration error in predicted risk
# For survival models, the expected absolute calibration error depends on
# the estimation precision of the baseline hazard and coefficients.
# Riley et al. specify that the margin of error in average predicted risk
# at prediction horizon should be approximately ±0.05

# This is related to the precision of the model's predictions. 
# A standard approximation: margin_of_error ≈ sqrt(p / events)
# For the given event rate and follow-up, we also consider the calibration window

# Time-adjusted calibration error (accounting for prediction horizon relative to follow-up)
time_ratio <- prediction_horizon / mean_followup
base_calibration_error <- sqrt(p / events_calculated)
adjusted_calibration_error <- base_calibration_error * time_ratio

cat("Base calibration error (sqrt(p/events)):", base_calibration_error, "\n")
cat("Time-adjusted calibration error (prediction horizon / mean follow-up):", 
    adjusted_calibration_error, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", target_margin_error, "\n")
cat("Criterion 2 (calibration margin) MET:", 
    adjusted_calibration_error <= target_margin_error, "\n\n")

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell

          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
